column1: # .github/codeql-register.tsv — the reviewed record of every CodeQL finding.
# Regenerate with: scripts/codeql-register.sh --refresh <sarif-dir>
# Policy, verdict vocabulary and fingerprint scheme: scripts/codeql-register.sh
# verdict: real | false-positive | deliberate | unreviewed
# A critical/high finding that is `real` or `unreviewed` FAILS the gate and
# blocks the release — such code is never built into an image. Medium and low
# are reported and must still carry a verdict, but do not block.
# There is deliberately no `blocked` verdict: this is code we wrote, so a fix
# is always available, and an undecided fix is an unmade decision rather than
# an unavailable one.
# Accepted findings are ALSO annotated at the site in the source. Where a
# verdict depends on a condition the fingerprint cannot see — an adjacent line,
# a caller, a config value — the reasoning must carry an explicit TRIP-WIRE
# note naming it.
# 'line' is navigation only and is refreshed each run; it is NOT part of the
# identity. The fingerprint is sha256(rule, path, CodeQL's line-content hash),
# so a finding that MOVES keeps its verdict and a finding whose flagged line is
# EDITED resets to unreviewed.

column8: Verification really is off and this really is TOFU. Safe to ship because the connection carries nothing and grants nothing: the request is an unauthenticated GET of /api/bmc?opt=get&type=about, VerifyPeerCertificate only RECORDS the fingerprint and always returns nil, and the captured digest is shown to the operator to confirm against the board before it becomes the pin NewTuringPiBackend enforces. TRIP-WIRE: void if this probe ever sends credentials, or if its result configures anything without the operator confirming the digest.

Certificate pinning is STRICTER than the CA trust being skipped: CA trust accepts any cert a trusted issuer signed, pinnedCertVerifier accepts exactly one SHA-256 fingerprint. Skipping is also not optional - the board mints a self-signed cert at the epoch, so it is permanently expired and no chain check can pass. TRIP-WIRE: safety lives on the NEXT line (tlsCfg.VerifyPeerCertificate = pinnedCertVerifier). If that assignment is removed, made conditional, or replaced with a partial comparison, this becomes accept-any-certificate and this fingerprint will NOT catch it.

Certificate pinning, which is STRICTER than the chain check it skips (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#448): chain trust accepts any certificate a trusted issuer signed; the VerifyConnection callback assigned beside this line in pinnedTLSConfig accepts exactly one public key, by the SHA-256 of the leaf SubjectPublicKeyInfo compared with the node's bus pin, and fails the handshake for anything else. Skipping the chain is required by design: the bus certificate is self-signed, and validity dates must not decide bus membership on a Pi that boots before NTP. Proven, not asserted, in agent/internal/bus/pinned_tls_config_test.go: TestPinnedTLSConfig_RefusesADifferentKeyInARealHandshake (a server with a different key is refused), TestPinnedTLSConfig_RefusesAServerWithNoCertificate (no certificate is refused), TestPinnedTLSConfig_PinCheckRunsOnResumedSessions (a resumed session still runs the pin check; verified to FAIL if the check is moved to VerifyPeerCertificate), and TestPinnedTLSConfig_TripWire_NeverSkipsVerificationWithoutAPinCheck; plus agent/internal/bus/pin_test.go TestClient_PinnedTLS and api/internal/bustls/functional_test.go TestFunctional_OfferMode with the real agent binary. TRIP-WIRE: this verdict lives on the VerifyConnection assignment, which the fingerprint does not cover — if it is removed, made conditional, or stops comparing the full digest, this line accepts any server; the trip-wire test above is what notices.

column8: Not password hashing. Every stored verifier is sha256 of a token GenerateToken produced - 32 bytes from crypto/rand, 256 bits, hex-encoded - minted here by MintBound or offline by rasputin-provision and loaded as a preseed hash by PreloadHashes. The flow CodeQL reports is Validate hashing the join token a connecting client presents as its NATS password (callout.go): network input, but only ever looked up against those verifiers, so what an attacker must guess is a 256-bit random value. Slow KDFs exist to make brute-force expensive against LOW-entropy human-chosen secrets; a 256-bit random token has no searchable keyspace, so argon2/bcrypt would buy nothing and would add cost to every bus authentication. TRIP-WIRE: void the moment a verifier is stored for an operator-typed secret, whether through HashToken, PreloadHashes or anything else. Today HashToken's callers are GenerateToken (used by MintBound and rasputin-provision) and Validate, and PreloadHashes stores only the hashes rasputin-provision got from GenerateToken. The passkey session store (api/internal/auth/store.go) also hashes session cookie tokens with it; those are 32 bytes from crypto/rand (auth.randomToken), the same premise.

False on two independent grounds. (1) No secret is present: CodeQL's paths start at ListPreAuthKeys and reach HashObserved through the observed-state map reconcileFetch builds in api/internal/mesh/jobs.go (HashObserved's only caller), and that per-key map copies only user, reusable, ephemeral and tags - never the key's ID or Plaintext, so key material never enters it. CodeQL tainted on the type NAME, not a value. (2) Not password hashing: this is a change-detection fingerprint reconcile compares desired against observed with, and nothing is ever verified against it. TRIP-WIRE: ground 1 holds only while the map reconcileFetch hashes stays metadata-only; copying a real key or token into it, or a new HashObserved caller that passes one, re-opens this.

column8: The flagged sink is not an open: it is the parent.Name()+"/"+name label OpenDir passes to os.NewFile, a display name for a directory fd that is already open. The open itself is the Openat just above, which takes ONE path component relative to an already-opened directory fd with O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY, then fstats and requires a directory: the kernel resolves the name beneath that fd and a symlink in it is ELOOP, so the primitive can only ever open a child of the fd it was handed, never a path. Whether a caller may name that child is the caller's shape check — the restore validates archive members and generation ids (validateRestorePath, proto.BackupValidGenerationID) and the ingest endpoint validates member paths by shape (proto.BackupValidMemberPath) before calling it. The taint CodeQL follows is the restore request's generation id, which PrepareRestore has already refused unless proto.BackupValidGenerationID accepts it, and which is opened relative to the generations directory. Covered by backupxfer/fsat tests (symlink refused at every position) and the restore's hostile-member cases.

The scheme is not attacker-reachable: the template literal hard-codes an http:// prefix, so the value can never begin with javascript: or data:, which is the only route from URL to script execution. firewallHost is operator-typed only - useState(empty), set solely by this input onChange - and the API-derived nodeId feeds the PLACEHOLDER, which is inert. TRIP-WIRE: the file comment says host derivation becomes automatic when primaryLanIp lands on Node; on that day this value becomes NODE-SUPPLIED and this verdict must be re-opened. The hard-coded scheme still caps it at open-redirect, not XSS.
